after: ## Claims before the European Court of Human Rights
alt: Four court formations from largest to smallest: a Grand Chamber of seventeen for the most serious issues, a Chamber of seven, a committee of three and a single judge, who can only declare clearly inadmissible applications inadmissible. The Court belongs to the Council of Europe, has been a single full-time court since Protocol 11, and has one judge per state.
caption: Strasbourg is a Council of Europe court with four formations.

after: ## Claims before the European Court of Human Rights
alt: Individual victims apply under Article 34 and states under Article 33 (Ireland v UK). A narrowing funnel of Article 35 admissibility criteria: domestic remedies exhausted, application within four months, not anonymous or repeated, not manifestly ill-founded, and a significant disadvantage. Only then is the case examined on the merits. Rule 39 interim measures can be used in urgent cases.
caption: A victim, exhausted remedies and four months: most applications fail at admissibility.

after: ## The effect of decisions on states and claimants
alt: A violation leads to just satisfaction under Article 41, and under Article 46 the Committee of Ministers supervises execution through individual measures for the claimant and general measures to prevent repetition. A table of UK responses: Sunday Times to the Contempt of Court Act 1981, Malone to the Interception of Communications Act 1985, Goodwin to the Gender Recognition Act 2004, S and Marper to the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012; after Hirst the UK delayed over a decade.
caption: Judgments bind states, and usually change UK law, but execution can be slow.

alt: Four HRA sections. Section 6: public authorities, core and hybrid, must act compatibly (YL v Birmingham City Council, reversed by the Care Act 2014). Section 7: only a victim may claim, normally within one year. Section 8: a just and appropriate remedy, with damages only where necessary (Greenfield). Section 2: courts take Strasbourg case law into account (Ullah; Horncastle).
caption: Who is bound, who may sue, what remedy, and how far to follow Strasbourg.

alt: Six stages of judicial review: a pre-action letter; a claim form in the Administrative Court promptly and within three months; standing, meaning sufficient interest or victim status for HRA claims; permission if there is an arguable case; a full hearing on illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety (CCSU), with proportionality where Convention rights are engaged (Daly); and discretionary remedies such as a quashing order.
caption: Letter, claim, standing, permission, grounds, remedy: six stages with filters along the way.

alt: Jo’s case in six steps: judicial review in the Administrative Court relying on Article 10; she is a victim under section 7(3); a pre-action letter then a claim within three months; grounds of illegality and proportionality (Daly); a quashing order and declaration, with damages only if needed (Greenfield); and, if she loses domestically, Strasbourg within four months.
caption: Domestic courts first, with tight time limits; Strasbourg is the last resort.
